title: Ang 537: Bihagra begins
tomorrow: what does longing sound like when it can't sleep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the passing world: love that says mine can't come along at the end, and the ninth Guru pointing to God's songs instead. He's back today, in a new raga.

At night the questions get bigger. Where am I going? Does any of this make sense? Is anybody steering? Bihagra, a raga tradition sings at night, opens on ang 537 with Guru Tegh Bahadur saying it flatly: nobody knows the Lord's ways. Yogis, ascetics, and plenty of clever people have worn themselves out trying. So if nobody can know, why keep trying? Sikhs answer that in more than one way.
screen: `THE BIG QUESTIONS AT NIGHT.` → `NOBODY KNOWS THE LORD'S WAYS.` → `SO WHY KEEP TRYING?`

segments.voice: First the hymn, in paraphrase: no one knows the Lord's ways. Yogis, celibates and ascetics have exhausted themselves, and so have many clever people. In an instant he turns a beggar into a king, and a king into a beggar. He fills what's empty, and empties what's full. That's the night raga's opening: not an answer, but a longing that knows it won't be answered on its own terms. Now, the two ways people read it. One reading says: stop grasping. The best case is right in the text. The cleverest people wore themselves out. Knowing was never the way in. What's left is to let go, take refuge, and trust the One whose ways you can't map. The other reading says: keep seeking. Its best case is the Granth itself. The Gurus knew no one could know, and they kept singing anyway, page after page, raga after raga. Not-knowing doesn't make the search pointless; it makes it endless. You can want what you can't hold. Both readings agree on one thing: the longing stays. Neither one says quit. Only how to carry it: with open hands, or with open eyes. That's night longing.
screen: `NOBODY KNOWS THE LORD'S WAYS.` · `THE CLEVER WEAR THEMSELVES OUT.` · `ONE READING: STOP GRASPING.` · `ANOTHER: KEEP SEEKING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `NIGHT LONGING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or lower them, and let one big question come up, the kind that shows up at night. Don't answer it. Sit with the wanting-to-know itself for the whole sit; if you'd like, read the ninth Guru's hymn on ang 537 first.
Ang 537. Where Bihagra begins, with the ninth Guru saying no one knows the Lord's ways, not even the clever.
Night longing: wanting what you can't fully know, and staying with it anyway. Sleep well when it's time.
